previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for a scheduled IVIG infusion using Privigen, a low osmolar agent, due to prior adverse reactions with other formulations. During the infusion, he developed hypertension with systolic pressure up to 200 and transient chest tightness, which was distinct from his usual anginal symptoms and not associated with EKG changes. He also experienced dizziness and a delayed episode of chest tightness and shortness of breath, which resolved without intervention. His blood pressure was managed by slowing the infusion rate, and no medication changes were made. His mitochondrial myopathy and cardiac conditions remained stable. Mild acidosis and dehydration improved with supportive care. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up on blood pressure and discuss infusion tolerance with his allergist.

#Hypogammaglobulinemia. Mr. ___ presented on the day of 
admission (___) for his scheduled IVIG dose for recently 
diagnosed hypogammaglobulinemia.  Given his issues with fluid 
balance secondary to mitochondrial disease, and his responses to 
prior IVIG doses, he required inpatient observation after IVIG 
administration.  On the night of admission, he received 1900cc 
of NS at 250cc/hr for the first 1000cc and 125cc/hr for the next 
___.  One hour prior to administration of IVIG on hospital day 
2 (___), he was pre-medicated with Benadryl 25mg and Tylenol 
___.  IgG subclasses were also checked prior to IVIG 
administration, revealing slightly decreased levels of IgG 
subclasses 1 and 3.  15 g IVIG were then administered per 
standard pharmacy protocol.  The patient developed some chest 
tightness, shortness of breath, nausea and headache that day 
which resolved by hospital day 3.  ECG and serial troponins were 
not concerning for cardiac ischemia, and his symptoms were 
similar to those he experienced after previous IVIG infusions.  
His symptoms resolved by the morning of ___, and the patient 
felt that he was ready to return home and was discharged.
.
#CAD/stable angina. The patient has a history of multiple stent 
placement, and 2x MIs, most recently in ___.  On the 
morning of admission, he had symptoms of chest tightness, 
diaphoresis, nausea, and feeling faint that, as per the patient, 
he regularly feels secondary to dehydration and is his baseline. 
 As stated above, he also developed chest tightness, dyspnea and 
nausea following his IVIG infusion.  Two EKGs showed no interval 
changes, and serial troponins were negative.  His symptoms were 
consistent with stable angina.  While in the hospital, we 
continued his home medications of aspirin, Plavix, metoprolol, 
ranexa.
.
#Mitochondrial disease.  The patient has been receiving ___ x 
per week NS boluses for orthostatic hypotension as an 
outpatient, secondary to disease.  In the hospital, the patient 
was given 1900cc NS prior to his IVIG administration as 
recommended by his PCP.
.
#LLE skin lesion. A skin lesion was noted on the patient's LLE 
that most likely represented an eczematous lesion.  As per the 
patient, this lesion has been growing over the past month.  
Given his history of squamous cell carcinoma, we recommended a 
follow-up outpatient appt with his dermatologist.

Dear Mr. ___,

You came into the hospital on ___ for a scheduled IVIG 
infusion for your hypogammaglobulinemia. You received the IVIG 
on ___ and were watched carefully for adverse reactions.  
You did have some chest tightness, shortness of breath, nausea 
and headache after IVIG which resolved with time. We checked an 
ECG which did not show any cardiac ischemia, and we drew cardiac 
enzyme blood labs which were negative for any signs of ischemia. 
We have very low suspcicion the pain was related to your heart, 
but if you experience recurrent pain that is new or different 
from your chronic pain we suggest you seek immediate evaluation. 


Given that you feel well this morning with no signficant 
residual symptoms from your infusion, you are ready to go home. 

No changes were made to your medications.

We recommend that you follow-up with your already scheduled 
appointments listed below in the follow-up section.

We have also printed out your pertinent lab results from this 
admission for your own records.
